description:
Hi, I’m Natalie! I’m a graphic designer, entrepreneur, and lifelong animal lover. My journey has taken me from running a business in Asia to New York City’s Mayor’s Office of Appointments. Watching Neil Armstrong walk on the Moon as a child sparked my lifelong fascination with space. I independently created Vitruvius Loom to bring forgotten space exploration machines to life for a new generation.

Space belongs to everyone.
summary:
Vitruvius Loom is an interactive 3D educational experience that invites curious children ages 8–13 to explore the machines humanity left on the Moon and Mars.

The journey begins beneath tonight’s real sky. Through a telescope, children join Manny, a present-day Lakota boy, in exploring the universe. Clicking the Moon launches a flight to NASA’s Tranquility Base, where Apollo 11 landed. There, explorers encounter Eagle’s descent stage, the Laser Ranging Retroreflector, still used for scientific measurements, and the Passive Seismic Experiment. They can hear authentic Apollo 12 seismic recordings and ask Ginny, an AI guide accompanied by NASA’s Ingenuity helicopter, questions answered with verified NASA sources.

Vitruvius Loom was conceived around a fundamental belief: intellectual potential is universal, but educational opportunity is not. Children growing up in rural communities, underserved neighborhoods, or households with limited financial resources deserve opportunities to engage with science, technology, and discovery. Their curiosity is no less valuable, their questions no less important, and their capacity to imagine no less extraordinary.

By making space exploration engaging, understandable, and accessible, Vitruvius Loom seeks to bridge educational divides, inspire scientific curiosity, and help children envision futures beyond the circumstances into which they were born.

Space belongs to everyone.
details:
We left a lander on the Moon. A mirror. A seismometer. On Mars, a helicopter that flew seventy-two times and then stopped.

Ask an eleven-year-old about any of it. They have never heard of it. If they had, they would call it junk.

Vitruvius Loom is for that kid. It looks like a telescope. It is a door.

You look through it at the real sky above your house tonight. You click the Moon. It zooms — and keeps zooming, past where a telescope should stop, down through real NASA terrain, until you are standing at Tranquility Base. Nothing cuts. Everything you walk on is real data.

Manny is waiting there. He is twelve, Lakota, hand-drawn, looking up at the same sky you are. He walks out to the machines on his own and reacts the way a kid reacts. He also tells you he is a simulation, because real data deserves real labels.

Manny has a guide of his own. Her name is Ginny, and Ginny is the helicopter — Ingenuity. Four pounds. Knee-high to a twelve-year-old. Five flights planned, seventy-two flown, grounded on Mars with a broken blade. The abandoned thing is the one who answers. She is held to 73 facts checked against NASA and the Smithsonian, shows her source every time, and says plainly when she does not know.

Play a real moonquake, recorded by Apollo 12's seismometer, and the instrument shakes in time with it.

And you are not dressed for it. Nobody who walks into another world ever is. So that is what comes next: kids build the suit — a second skin, laced and stitched to press evenly on the body, designed against what they just learned.

No account. No login. No lesson. No quiz. No score. It runs in a browser on a tablet, and every answer shows its source — which teaches a second thing underneath the first: how to tell a checked fact from a confident guess.

Space is taught as launches. The rocket goes up, the story ends, and a child who gets curious once has nowhere to take it. This is the second step.

But curiosity is not distributed according to income, geography, or access to opportunity. A child growing up in a rural community, an underserved neighborhood, or a household with limited financial resources is no less capable of scientific inquiry than a child attending a well-funded school with a robotics laboratory. What differs is exposure, access, and the opportunity to discover what is possible.

Vitruvius Loom begins with the belief that scientific exploration should not be reserved for those who can afford specialized equipment, expensive programs, or travel to museums and space centers. By bringing an immersive, source-based experience into an ordinary web browser, the project seeks to make the universe more approachable to children who might otherwise never encounter these discoveries.

It does not replace teachers, museums, or hands-on scientific education. It offers another doorway into learning, one that invites children to investigate, question, imagine, and recognize that the history and future of space exploration belong to them, too.

Space belongs to everyone.

Built with React, TypeScript, three.js, React Three Fiber, and Cesium for Moon and Mars terrain. Data: JPL Horizons, HEASARC (9,096 stars), NASA/USGS terrain, NASA models of the Lunar Module and Ingenuity, the Apollo 12 seismic recording, ESA data for Mars. Ginny runs on Google Gemini via Vertex AI; voices are Kokoro; Manny came from scribbled sketch , propped with AI, following into 3D with Meshy. ChatGPT, Claude and AI imaging tools helped write code, draft text and prepare art. Hosted on Google Cloud Run behind Cloudflare. A browser is all it needs.

The door is the idea: nothing cuts, so the scale does the teaching. And the objects narrate themselves — one of them literally does.

Accuracy over fluency: a guide that improvises about Apollo is worse than none, so Ginny must decline. Honesty: Manny says he is a simulation, and every AI tool is named. Respect: his Lakota is read by a Lakota reader. Privacy: no accounts, nothing stored, any question with a name, email or address blocked before it sends. Performance: a tablet, not a workstation.

That mirror has been returning laser light to Earth since 1969. Most children have never been told it exists. It is time they did.
